subject: English
description: Past perfect, present perfect continuous, future perfect, conditional tenses

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'By the time we arrived, the train ___ already.'

options.option_text: left
had left
has left
leaves

questions.explanation: Two past events — earlier one in PAST PERFECT ('had left'), later in simple past ('arrived'). Pattern: 'By the time + past, past perfect had happened'. Distractor 1 — simple past loses the sequence. Distractor 3 — present perfect (mismatch with past time). Distractor 4 — simple present.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'She ___ at this company since 2018.'

options.option_text: is working at the firm
has been working there
was working last year
had worked previously

questions.explanation: Action started in past + still continuing → PRESENT PERFECT CONTINUOUS ('has been working'). Trigger words: SINCE, FOR. Distractor 1 — present continuous misses 'since 2018'. Distractor 3 — past continuous suggests it ended. Distractor 4 — simple present misses duration.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'By next year, they ___ ten years of marriage.'

options.option_text: complete a decade together
will have completed a decade
are completing a decade now
had completed a decade then

questions.explanation: FUTURE PERFECT — 'will have + past participle' for an action that will be completed by a specific point in the future. Pattern: 'By + future time, will have done'. Distractor 1 — simple present. Distractor 3 — present continuous. Distractor 4 — present perfect (no future reference).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'If I ___ the lottery, I would buy a house.'

options.option_text: win
won
had won
will win

questions.explanation: SECOND CONDITIONAL — hypothetical/unlikely present-future. Pattern: 'If + simple past, would + base verb'. Use 'won' (subjunctive past form). Distractor 1 — first conditional (real possibility), would need 'will buy', not 'would buy'. Distractor 3 — third conditional (past unreal), would need 'would have bought'. Distractor 4 — never used after 'if' in conditionals.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'If she had studied harder, she ___ the exam.'

options.option_text: would pass the difficult exam
would have passed the exam
passes the exam every time
will pass the exam tomorrow

questions.explanation: THIRD CONDITIONAL — past unreal / counterfactual. Pattern: 'If + past perfect, would have + past participle'. She didn't actually study harder, so the consequence is also counterfactual: 'would have passed'. Distractor 1 — second conditional ending. Distractor 3 — simple present. Distractor 4 — first conditional ending.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'I ___ for two hours when he finally called me.'

options.option_text: was waiting
had been waiting
have been waiting
waited

questions.explanation: PAST PERFECT CONTINUOUS — action that was ongoing for a duration up to a point in the past. Pattern: 'had been + V-ing'. Two past events: long action (waiting for 2 hours) BEFORE the shorter event (he called). Distractor 1 — past continuous loses the duration sense. Distractor 3 — present perfect continuous (current relevance). Distractor 4 — simple past loses the ongoing aspect.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Look! The kids ___ in the garden.'

options.option_text: play in the garden daily
are playing in the garden
played in the garden once
have played in the garden

questions.explanation: PRESENT CONTINUOUS — for actions happening RIGHT NOW. 'Look!' signals immediate observation → present continuous 'are playing'. Distractor 1 — simple present implies habitual action. Distractor 3 — past simple. Distractor 4 — present perfect (focus on result).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The River Brahmaputra _____ through Assam before joining the Ganga delta system in Bangladesh.

options.option_text: flows eastward through the plains region
is flowing through the flood-prone areas
has flowed through this region for ages
was flowing before the major dams were built

questions.explanation: A is correct because simple present is used for permanent geographical facts and universal truths. 'Is flowing' (B) wrongly implies a temporary ongoing action rather than a permanent state. 'Has flowed' (C) emphasises experience or result, not a permanent geographical fact. 'Was flowing' (D) is past continuous, which is incorrect for a fact that remains true today.

questions.stem: ISRO scientists _____ the Chandrayaan-3 mission successfully in July 2023.

options.option_text: have accomplished the historic lunar feat
accomplished the lunar landing that very month
had accomplished the mission with great effort
were accomplishing the mission at that launch

questions.explanation: B is correct because past simple is mandatory when a specific past time marker ('in July 2023') is present. Present perfect (A) is incompatible with definite past time references — the most common candidate error. Past perfect (C) is wrong as there is no earlier past reference point to relate back to. Past continuous (D) is incorrect because the launch was a discrete completed event, not an ongoing background action at the time.

questions.stem: This time tomorrow, the Prime Minister _____ the new national highway project in Uttarakhand.

options.option_text: will have inaugurated the highway project
inaugurates the new infrastructure project
will be inaugurating the highway project
would inaugurate the highway project then

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'this time tomorrow' signals an action in progress at a specified future moment, requiring future continuous. Future perfect (A) implies the action will be fully completed by that time, not in progress — a precise but common mix-up. Present simple (B) can mark scheduled events but is less precise than future continuous with 'this time tomorrow'. 'Would' (D) marks a conditional, not a future tense.

questions.stem: The officer declared, 'We are investigating the fraud case.' Identify the correctly reported version: 'The officer declared that they _____ the fraud case.'

options.option_text: are investigating at that very moment
were investigating the fraud case then
had been investigating well before the raid
investigate such cases on a regular basis

questions.explanation: B is correct: with a past reporting verb ('declared'), present continuous backshifts to past continuous — 'are investigating' becomes 'were investigating'. Option A retains the original tense without backshift, violating reported speech rules. Option C uses past perfect continuous, which is the backshift for original past continuous forms only, not present continuous — a sophisticated trap. Option D drops the continuous aspect entirely, distorting the original meaning.

questions.stem: The auditors discovered that the firm _____ its financial accounts for three consecutive years.

options.option_text: manipulates the accounts every fiscal quarter
was manipulating accounts at the audit point
had manipulated the accounts quite deliberately
has manipulated accounts over many recent years

questions.explanation: C is correct because the manipulation occurred and concluded before the act of discovery, requiring past perfect ('had manipulated') to establish that earlier sequence. Option A uses present simple, which is tense-inconsistent with the past verb 'discovered'. Option B (past continuous) suggests the manipulation was still actively happening at the moment of discovery, losing the sense of completed prior wrongdoing. Option D (present perfect) cannot follow a past simple verb like 'discovered' in the same narrative timeline.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences correctly uses a stative verb in its appropriate tense form?

options.option_text: She is knowing the answer to this tricky problem
He has been owning this property since the year 2010
They have known each other since their childhood
We are believing in the power of good education

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'know' is a stative verb expressing a mental state, and present perfect simple ('have known') correctly describes a state that began in the past and continues to the present. Options A and D use the stative verbs 'know' and 'believe' in the present continuous form — stative verbs (mental states, emotions, possession, senses) cannot take continuous aspect. Option B misuses 'own' (possession = stative) in the present perfect continuous form, which is equally incorrect and a popular examiner trap.

questions.stem: The examination board's directive mandates that every candidate _____ a valid photo identity proof on the day of the written test.

options.option_text: carries the valid photo identity document
carry a valid and acceptable identity proof
is carrying a photo identity proof at all times
carried the identity document on that test day

questions.explanation: B is correct because verbs of mandate, command, or recommendation ('mandate', 'insist', 'recommend', 'propose') require the present subjunctive in the following that-clause — the base (infinitive) form for all persons, hence 'carry' not 'carries'. Option A is the primary trap: candidates apply normal subject-verb agreement (third-person 's') without recognising the subjunctive mood triggered by 'mandate that'. Option C (present continuous) and Option D (past tense) are both tense-structurally incompatible with the subjunctive construction.

questions.stem: Which form correctly completes the sentence: 'The director ___ with the committee's recommendation, so the proposal was approved unanimously'?

options.option_text: is agreeing fully with the recommendation
agrees completely with the recommendation
was agreeing on all the recommendations
had been agreeing with their suggestions

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'agree' is a stative verb expressing a mental state; stative verbs do not normally take the progressive form. Options A ('is agreeing') and C ('was agreeing') wrongly use continuous tenses with a stative verb — a classic exam trap. Option D ('had been agreeing') implies a prolonged past action that stopped at a specific point, which is unnatural for stative verbs and clashes with the simple past context of the main clause.

questions.stem: In response to the question 'Have you submitted the project report yet?', which reply is grammatically correct?

options.option_text: No, I did not submit the report yet
No, I have not submitted the report yet
No, I was not submitting the report yet
No, I had not submitted the report yet

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'yet' in negative statements pairs with the present perfect (have/has + past participle) to indicate an action not completed up to the present moment. Option A ('did not submit yet') is the most common error — simple past cannot combine with 'yet' in a present-time context. Option D ('had not submitted') would be appropriate only in a past narrative where 'yet' referred to a past cut-off point, not the present.

questions.stem: Riya has already bought the ingredients for tonight's dinner. Which sentence correctly expresses her pre-planned intention?

options.option_text: Riya will cook dinner for the guests tonight
Riya is going to cook dinner for guests tonight
Riya cooks dinner for all the guests tonight
Riya would cook dinner for the guests tonight

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'be going to + infinitive' expresses a pre-planned intention backed by present evidence (the already-purchased ingredients). Option A ('will cook') signals a spontaneous decision made at the moment of speaking, not a prior arrangement — a key distinction examiners frequently test. Option C (simple present 'cooks') is reserved for fixed timetables or habitual routines, not personal plans. Option D ('would cook') is a conditional or reported-speech form and is inappropriate here.

questions.stem: Which option correctly fills the blank: 'The forensic team realised that the key evidence ___ before their arrival, complicating the entire case'?

options.option_text: was already destroyed by unknown persons
had already been destroyed by someone
is already being destroyed at the scene
has already been destroyed since then

questions.explanation: B is correct because the evidence was destroyed before the team arrived — when two past actions occur in sequence, the earlier one requires the past perfect ('had been destroyed'). Option A ('was destroyed') uses simple past, which cannot clearly establish that the destruction preceded the arrival. Option D ('has been destroyed') is present perfect, anchored to the present, and cannot frame a completed event within a past narrative. Option C ('is being destroyed') wrongly uses the present continuous.

questions.stem: The coach announced, 'My players are completely exhausted.' Which of the following reports this statement correctly in indirect speech?

options.option_text: The coach announced that his players were completely exhausted
The coach announced that his players are completely exhausted
The coach announced that his players had been exhausting
The coach told that his players were completely exhausted

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'announced' is a past reporting verb, so the present 'are' backshifts to 'were' following the sequence-of-tenses rule. Option B retains the present tense 'are', violating the backshift rule — permissible only for universal truths, which does not apply here. Option C changes the meaning ('exhausting' means causing fatigue, not feeling it). Option D is the subtlest trap: 'told' requires an indirect object ('told them that…'); without one, 'said that' must be used instead.

questions.stem: Which form correctly completes the formal sentence: 'The geological survey ___ its assessment before the monsoon begins, or the construction tender cannot be awarded'?

options.option_text: would have completed the full assessment
will have completed its full assessment
has completed the entire assessment now
shall be completing the assessment timely

questions.explanation: B is correct: future perfect ('will have + past participle') expresses an action that will be completed before a specified future moment ('before the monsoon begins'). Option A ('would have completed') is the conditional perfect, used in hypothetical or third-conditional contexts — not for a straightforward future deadline. Option C ('has completed') is present perfect, anchored to the present rather than the future. Option D ('shall be completing') is future continuous, signalling an action in progress at a future time, not its completion before a deadline.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly uses an inverted conditional to show that a past unfulfilled action has led to a present consequence?

options.option_text: Should stricter norms have been followed, fewer accidents occur now
Had stricter norms been followed, fewer accidents would occur now
Were stricter norms to be followed, fewer accidents would have occurred
Had stricter norms been followed, fewer accidents would have occurred

questions.explanation: B is the inverted mixed conditional: 'Had + subject + past participle' (past unfulfilled condition) + 'would + base verb + now' (present consequence). Option A ('Should…') inverts the first conditional for unlikely but possible future events, not a past unfulfilled condition. Option C ('Were…to be') is the inverted second conditional for present hypotheticals, and 'would have occurred' wrongly places the result in the past. Option D is the most tempting distractor: it is a valid inverted third conditional, but 'would have occurred' puts the consequence in the past, not the present — failing the 'present consequence' criterion.
